question.prompt: For which customer need does Mara recommend printing?
question.explanation: Mara explicitly recommends printing for inexpensive temporary signs. Her preference depends on the purpose rather than a universal opposition to one technique.

stimulus.title: Interview with a sign painter
stimulus.body:
Interviewer: You still paint shop signs by hand. Is that because you dislike computers?

Mara: No. I use a computer to send drafts and manage orders. A brush gives a different edge to a letter, and some customers want that. Others need inexpensive temporary signs, so I recommend printing.

Interviewer: Did you always have such steady hands?

Mara: My first letters leaned like tired fence posts. My teacher made me paint straight lines for a week. I thought I was being punished. Later I realised she was giving me control of the brush before asking me to control a whole word.

Interviewer: What is the hardest part now?

Mara: Listening before drawing. A bakery once asked for an old-fashioned sign. I pictured dark green and gold. The owner meant the bright red lettering her grandmother used. We would have agreed on the words 'old-fashioned' and disagreed completely about the picture. Now I ask for examples before choosing a colour.

workedSolution: Mara explicitly recommends printing for inexpensive temporary signs.
Her preference depends on the purpose rather than a universal opposition to one technique.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

question.prompt: What must the tower do before its height is measured?

stimulus.title: Instructions for a paper tower test
stimulus.body:
Your group has six sheets of paper and fifty centimetres of tape. Build a tower that stands without support for ten seconds. Before building, record your planned base width. You may fold or roll paper, but you may not attach the tower to the table.

Measure height only after the tower has stood for ten seconds. If it falls earlier, record the attempt as unstable, not as a height of zero. Zero suggests no height was built, whereas unstable describes a different problem. You may then rebuild with the same materials, recording any changes.

When comparing attempts, look at both height and stability. A very tall tower that falls after three seconds does not meet the task. A lower tower that stands may provide a useful starting point for another design. Do not conclude from one successful attempt that a design will always work. Repeat the test and note whether a slight change in placement affects the result.

stimulus.title: Instructions for a paper tower test
stimulus.body:
Your group has six sheets of paper and fifty centimetres of tape. Build a tower that stands without support for ten seconds. Before building, record your planned base width. You may fold or roll paper, but you may not attach the tower to the table.

Measure height only after the tower has stood for ten seconds. If it falls earlier, record the attempt as unstable, not as a height of zero. Zero suggests no height was built, whereas unstable describes a different problem. You may then rebuild with the same materials, recording any changes.

When comparing attempts, look at both height and stability. A very tall tower that falls after three seconds does not meet the task. A lower tower that stands may provide a useful starting point for another design. Do not conclude from one successful attempt that a design will always work. Repeat the test and note whether a slight change in placement affects the result.
